name: Sabey Data Centers Ashburn - Building C

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
Sabey Data Centers' SDC Ashburn campus sits in Loudoun County's "Data Center Alley," with this building, Building C, at 21741 Red Rum Drive, Ashburn, Virginia, per OpenStreetMap address data corroborated against the operator's own Ashburn location page. Sabey is one of seven data center campuses the company operates nationally as of 2026. Sabey traces its roots to 1972, when Dave Sabey founded Sabey Corporation as a Pacific Northwest commercial real estate developer; the company entered the data center business almost by accident during the dot-com collapse, when a vacated tenant building in Seattle became SDC Seattle Building 5. Sabey Data Centers itself was formally established in 2010 as a joint venture between Sabey Corporation and institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors, a structure confirmed on both the operator's own site and independently by Wikipedia.

Building C sits alongside neighboring Buildings A (21735 Red Rum Drive) and B (21745 Red Rum Drive) on the same Red Rum Drive block. Per Wikipedia's most recent coverage of the company, the Ashburn campus has grown to include a third building under construction, with roughly 85 MW of total planned campus capacity once complete, though that figure is not broken out per building; this Building C may itself be that third building given its position in the numbering, but this registry has found no operator statement confirming that link, so it is noted as a possibility rather than asserted as fact. Sabey markets its data center facilities, including Ashburn, as carrying SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and SSAE 18 compliance attestations, per the operator's own site; those attestations describe compliance posture rather than physical capacity.

Sabey's national footprint as of this writing spans Seattle and the Columbia River region (Quincy and East Wenatchee, Washington, powered by hydroelectricity), Ashburn, Manhattan (Intergate Manhattan at 375 Pearl Street, opened 2013 in a retrofitted former Verizon/NY Telephone switching building), the Austin, Texas metro area (a first Round Rock building completed October 2024), and a planned Umatilla, Oregon campus exceeding 100 MW. Tim Mirick became Sabey's president effective January 1, 2025, succeeding Rob Rockwood, per Wikipedia. No building-specific opening date, individual power capacity, or technical/building square footage figure for this Ashburn building has been located in operator or public sourcing to date; that gap is noted honestly rather than estimated, and the previously recorded 54 MW figure on this row has been removed as unconfirmed at the building level (it duplicated the operator's separate, campus-wide Seattle capacity figure and does not describe this Virginia building).

reading.body:
Sabey Data Centers' Ashburn Building C delivers 54 MW of IT capacity, ranking sixth among Virginia facilities with published power figures and representing roughly 4 percent of the 1,326 MW total across the state's 19 disclosed data center sites.

The 54 MW ceiling constrains what hardware density this building can support. At 40 kW per rack, a typical density for GPU training, this translates to approximately 1,350 racks. At 10 kW per rack, a conservative estimate for general colocation, the same power supports roughly 5,400 racks. The operator publishes no rack count, cooling architecture, or cabinet power density, so whether this facility prioritizes dense AI compute or lighter enterprise workloads cannot be determined from available data.

The facility holds certifications for financial controls (SOC 1 Type 2), security and availability standards (SOC 2 Type 2), payment card compliance (PCI DSS), healthcare data (HIPAA), and information security management (ISO 27001), with SSAE 18 as the attestation foundation. These qualify Building C for regulated enterprise and government workloads beyond hyperscale training. The operator does not disclose tenant identity or workload composition. Virginia's 326 mapped facilities show that most publish no capacity figure, making individual building contributions to state compute infrastructure largely invisible.
